```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(knitr)
library(scales)
library(patchwork)
library(MASS)
library(nnet)

# MASS::select masks dplyr's, and we want dplyr's everywhere below
select <- dplyr::select

knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "ragg_png")

# CASA palette, stated explicitly so the deck does not depend on casaviz
casa_purple <- "#4E3C56"
casa_teal   <- "#2E6260"
casa_yellow <- "#F9DD73"
casa_pink   <- "#E16FCA"
casa_green  <- "#9DBB65"
casa_red    <- "#C94C4C"
casa_cols   <- c("#2E6260", "#658E62", "#9DBB65", "#E7D870",
                 "#F3C486", "#E993AC", "#8F5289", "#4E3C56")

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 16))

base_path <- here("sessions", "L6_data", "Performancetables_130242", "2022-2023")

# The DfE publishes suppressed / not-applicable values as codes, not blanks
na_all <- c("", "NA", "SUPP", "NP", "NE", "SP", "SN", "LOWCOV", "NEW", "SUPPMAT")

# Every file is keyed on URN. The LA and national summary rows carry no URN,
# and because dplyr joins NA to NA they would duplicate rows as well as not
# being schools - so they go before anything else happens.
read_dfe <- function(f) {
  suppressWarnings(
    read_csv(file.path(base_path, f), na = na_all, show_col_types = FALSE)
  ) |>
    mutate(URN = as.character(URN)) |>
    filter(!is.na(URN))
}

ks4 <- read_dfe("england_ks4final.csv") |>
  select(URN, ATT8SCR, P8MEA, TPUP, PTFSM6CLA1A, TFSM6CLA1A, PTEALGRP2, PTPRIORHI) |>
  mutate(across(-URN, ~ parse_number(as.character(.x))))

absence <- read_dfe("england_abs.csv") |>
  distinct(URN, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  select(URN, PERCTOT, PPERSABS10) |>
  mutate(across(-URN, ~ parse_number(as.character(.x))))

school_info <- read_dfe("england_school_information.csv") |>
  select(URN, SCHNAME, LANAME, MINORGROUP, OFSTEDRATING, OFSTEDLASTINSP)

destinations <- read_dfe("england_ks4-pupdest.csv") |>
  distinct(URN, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  select(URN, COHORT, OVERALL_DEST) |>
  mutate(across(-URN, ~ parse_number(as.character(.x))))

# Mainstream secondaries with an Ofsted judgement. Ofsted's five published
# grades collapse to four analytical ones: "serious weaknesses" and "special
# measures" are both categories of inadequate in Ofsted's own scheme, and
# separately they are far too small to model.
schools <- ks4 |>
  inner_join(absence, by = "URN") |>
  inner_join(school_info, by = "URN") |>
  filter(MINORGROUP %in% c("Academy", "Maintained school"),
         OFSTEDRATING %in% c("Outstanding", "Good", "Requires improvement",
                             "Serious Weaknesses", "Special Measures")) |>
  mutate(
    rating4 = case_when(
      OFSTEDRATING == "Outstanding"           ~ "Outstanding",
      OFSTEDRATING == "Good"                  ~ "Good",
      OFSTEDRATING == "Requires improvement"  ~ "Requires improvement",
      TRUE                                    ~ "Inadequate"),
    rating4 = factor(rating4,
                     levels = c("Inadequate", "Requires improvement",
                                "Good", "Outstanding"),
                     ordered = TRUE),
    below_good  = as.integer(rating4 %in% c("Inadequate", "Requires improvement")),
    outstanding = as.integer(rating4 == "Outstanding"),
    insp_year   = suppressWarnings(as.integer(substr(OFSTEDLASTINSP, 7, 10)))
  )

model_data <- schools |>
  drop_na(P8MEA, PTFSM6CLA1A, PERCTOT, PPERSABS10, TPUP, PTPRIORHI)

# One split, used by every classification model in the deck
set.seed(42)
train_idx <- sample(nrow(model_data), floor(0.7 * nrow(model_data)))
train <- model_data[train_idx, ]
test  <- model_data[-train_idx, ]

# AUC by the rank identity, so the deck needs no extra package
auc_of <- function(scores, actual) {
  r  <- rank(scores)
  n1 <- sum(actual == 1); n0 <- sum(actual == 0)
  (sum(r[actual == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}

# Every model below spells its formula out in full rather than sharing one
# object. More typing, but the code on the slide is then exactly the code that
# runs, which matters more in a teaching deck than staying DRY.
```

## Recap {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

- Over three weeks we built a regression model up from a single scatter
  plot to a linear mixed effects model with random intercepts and random
  slopes
- We learned a **recipe** - understand your data, start simple, add
  complexity only when it earns its place, and check your assumptions at
  every step
- Last week we relaxed one particular assumption: that our observations
  were **independent**. Schools sit inside local authorities, and that
  grouping matters

## But one thing never changed {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

- Every single model we have fitted has had a **continuous outcome
  variable**
- Attainment 8. Progress 8. Numbers that can take any value, that are
  roughly bell-shaped, and that happily sit on either side of a straight
  line
- This choice let us use Ordinary Least Squares throughout - but we know
  that our data don't always look like this
- What happens when the thing you want to explain is a *yes/no*, a
  *category*, or a *count*?

## This week's session aims {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

- Understand why OLS fails when the outcome is not continuous, and see
  it fail
- Meet the **Generalised Linear Model (GLM)** - one framework, three
  moving parts
- **Logistic regression** for binary outcomes - in depth, because if you
  understand this one the rest follow
- Where **counts and ordered categories** fit in, and where to go for them
- **How to judge one** when there is no R² - deviance, AIC, the
  pseudo-R²s, and whether the predictions are actually any use
- Throughout: can we predict a school's Ofsted rating from everything
  else we know about it?

# Back to Week 1 {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## Remember these? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

In week 1 we spent a long time on **types of data**, and on the
**distributions** that go with them.

| Data type | Example from our data | Distribution |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Real-valued | Attainment 8 | Normal |
| Binary | Is this school single-sex? | Bernoulli / Binomial |
| Count | How many pupils on free school meals? | Poisson |
| Count, overdispersed | ... when the variance exceeds the mean | Negative binomial |
| Ordinal | Ofsted rating | *(no single answer)* |

. . .

We then spent three weeks modelling **only the first row**!

## The whole idea of a GLM, in one table {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

| If your outcome is... | ...its distribution is | ...the model is |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| A continuous number | Normal | **OLS** - weeks 5, 6, 7 |
| A yes/no | Binomial | **Logistic regression** |
| A proportion out of a known total | Binomial | **Logistic regression** |
| An ordered category | \- | **Ordinal logistic** |
| An unordered category | \- | **Multinomial logistic** |
| A count | Poisson | **Poisson regression** |
| A count that is too variable | Negative binomial | **Negative binomial regression** |

. . .

**This is not seven new methods.** It is one method, with a slot you
fill differently depending on what you are trying to explain.

## What actually changes {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Every GLM has exactly three pieces. You already know the middle one.

::: incremental
1.  **The random component** - what distribution does the outcome
    follow? (Normal, binomial, Poisson...)
2.  **The linear predictor** - $\beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + ...$
    . This is *identical* to everything we have done for three weeks
3.  **The link function** - the bit of maths that connects the two, so
    that a straight line on one scale becomes a sensible prediction on
    the other
:::

. . .

OLS is just the GLM where the distribution is Normal and the link
function does nothing at all.

## What a link function actually does {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Every regression we have fitted works the same way: take each predictor,
multiply it by a number, and add the results up.

$$y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + \dots$$

- The model is **just arithmetic**
- But arithmetic ignores the reality of your data
  - feed in a big enough $x$ and the sum ($y$) comes out as 14.2.
  - feed in a small enough $x$ and it comes out as $-3$.
- Both are perfectly good numbers
- But the thing we are *predicting* ($y$) is usually not free to be **any**
  number, even though the maths would allow it.
  - A probability can't be $-3$.
  - A count of schools can't be $-3$ either.
- **The sum on the right of the equation has more freedom than the
  outcome does**

## What a link function actually does {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
| Outcome | Its natural range | Link stretches it with | To get back, apply |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| A continuous number | $-\infty$ to $+\infty$ | *nothing needed* | *nothing* |
| A probability | 0 to 1 | $\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)$ | the logistic curve |
| A count | 0 to $+\infty$ | $\log$ | $\exp$ |
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
-   **The link is a translator.** It stretches a squashed natural range out onto the whole number line, so the straight line has somewhere sensible to live.
-   The top row needs no stretching, because a continuous outcome already has the same freedom the sum does
   —   which is exactly why **OLS is a GLM with the boring link**.
:::

## The same model, three times {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Written out in full, with the **right-hand side identical every time**. Only
the left changes.

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**Ordinary regression** — the outcome goes in as it is:

$$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + \dots + \epsilon_i$$
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**Logistic regression** — the *probability* goes in, through the logit:

$$\log\!\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + \dots$$
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**Poisson regression** — the *average count* goes in, through a log:

$$\log\big(E[y_i]\big) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + \dots$$

[$E[y_i]$ is standard notation for the **expected value** of $y$ — the average
count for a school like this one.]{style="font-size:0.85em; color:#666;"}
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.86em;"}
Notice what is **missing** from the bottom two: the $\epsilon$. OLS adds an
error term on the end; a GLM does not, because the randomness is already
described by the distribution you chose. **That is the swap** — an error term
for a distribution.
:::

## Without a link, and with one {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| label: link-vs-nolink
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.9
#| fig-align: center

# Counts, not probabilities - the binary version gets its own slide later, and
# this way the framing previews Poisson instead of repeating logistic.
la_link <- schools |>
  group_by(LANAME) |>
  summarise(n_below  = sum(below_good),
            mean_abs = mean(PERCTOT, na.rm = TRUE),
            n_schools = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n_schools >= 5, !is.na(mean_abs))

m_ols  <- lm(n_below ~ mean_abs, data = la_link)
m_pois <- glm(n_below ~ mean_abs, data = la_link, family = poisson)

grid_l <- tibble(mean_abs = seq(3.5, max(la_link$mean_abs) + 0.5, length.out = 200))
grid_l$ols  <- predict(m_ols,  newdata = grid_l)
grid_l$pois <- predict(m_pois, newdata = grid_l, type = "response")

shared <- list(
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = 0,
           fill = casa_red, alpha = 0.09),
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4),
  geom_point(data = la_link, aes(mean_abs, n_below),
             alpha = 0.35, colour = casa_purple, size = 1.3),
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-2.5, 23)),
  labs(x = "Average absence across the LA (%)", y = "Schools rated below Good"),
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
)

p_no <- ggplot() + shared +
  geom_line(data = grid_l, aes(mean_abs, ols), colour = casa_red, linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "No link: a straight line")

p_yes <- ggplot() + shared +
  geom_line(data = grid_l, aes(mean_abs, pois), colour = casa_teal, linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "Log link: a curve that cannot go below zero")

patchwork::wrap_plots(p_no, p_yes, nrow = 1)
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.82em"}
-   Same data, same predictor. The straight line is heading somewhere
impossible
—   follow it left and it promises a **negative number of schools**. 
-   The log link bends the same relationship so it flattens towards zero instead, and can never cross it.
:::

# Can we predict School Ofsted ratings? {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## Our question for today {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

- We have used Ofsted ratings as a **predictor** and as a **grouping
  variable** already
- Today we turn it around and make it the **outcome**
- *Given everything else we know about a school - its results, its
  intake, its absence rates, its size - can we predict what Ofsted said
  about it?*
- And if we can, what does that tell us about what Ofsted is actually
  measuring?
- **Note**, *Ofsted has changed how it rates schools now, so single-word ratings are no longer given*

## The outcome variable {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| out-width: 95%

model_data |>
  count(rating4) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = rating4, y = n, fill = rating4)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = comma(n)), vjust = -0.4, size = 5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(casa_red, casa_pink, casa_teal, casa_green)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Schools",
       title = "Ofsted ratings, mainstream secondaries in England") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
`r comma(nrow(model_data))` schools with complete data. Note immediately
how **lopsided** this is - we will come back to that, because it causes
more trouble than anything else today.
:::

## First attempt: just use OLS? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

- Let's re-code our ratings: "below Good" as **1** and "Good or better"
  as **0**
- We can regress it on Progress 8 exactly as we have been doing for the
  last three weeks.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
lpm <- lm(below_good ~ P8MEA, data = model_data)
summary(lpm)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
lpm_range <- range(fitted(lpm))
lpm_neg   <- sum(fitted(lpm) < 0)
# What the straight line predicts for a solidly above-average school, used in
# the caption on the next slide. Computed rather than typed so it cannot drift
# if the filters on model_data ever change.
p8_one    <- as.numeric(predict(lpm, newdata = data.frame(P8MEA = 1)))
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
The model runs. It produces coefficients. It produces an R². Nothing
errors.

**And its fitted values run from `r round(lpm_range[1], 3)` to
`r round(lpm_range[2], 3)`.**
:::

## A probability of minus fifty percent? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| out-width: 95%

grid <- tibble(P8MEA = seq(min(model_data$P8MEA), max(model_data$P8MEA), length.out = 300))
grid$lpm <- predict(lpm, newdata = grid)
glm1 <- glm(below_good ~ P8MEA, data = model_data, family = binomial)
grid$glm <- predict(glm1, newdata = grid, type = "response")

ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = 1, ymax = Inf,
           fill = casa_red, alpha = 0.08) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = 0,
           fill = casa_red, alpha = 0.08) +
  geom_jitter(data = model_data, aes(P8MEA, below_good),
              height = 0.03, alpha = 0.10, colour = casa_purple, size = 0.9) +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(P8MEA, lpm, colour = "Straight line (OLS)"), linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(P8MEA, glm, colour = "Logistic curve"), linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0, 1), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
  # Mark the single point the caption talks about, so it can be found on the
  # graph rather than taken on trust
  annotate("point", x = 1, y = p8_one, colour = casa_red, size = 3.2) +
  annotate("segment", x = 1, xend = 1.45, y = p8_one, yend = p8_one - 0.18,
           colour = casa_red, linewidth = 0.4) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = p8_one - 0.21, hjust = 0, size = 4,
           colour = casa_red,
           label = sprintf("Progress 8 = +1\npredicts %.0f%%", 100 * p8_one)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Straight line (OLS)" = casa_red,
                                 "Logistic curve" = casa_teal), name = NULL) +
  # The caption talks in percentages, so the axis does too - a probability
  # axis labelled 0.00-1.00 against a caption saying "-13%" invites exactly
  # the question of where the -13% is supposed to be
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(x = "Progress 8 score", y = "P(rated below Good)",
       title = "The shaded bands are impossible probabilities") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
- The straight line gives **`r comma(lpm_neg)` schools a negative
  probability** of being rated below good.
- At a Progress 8 of +1 it predicts a probability of being rated below
  good of about **`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * p8_one)`** (impossible).
- The logistic curve cannot do this - it is bounded at 0 and 1 by
  construction.
:::

## Where the curve comes from {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

We need something that takes a straight line, which runs from $-\infty$
to $+\infty$, and squashes it into $[0,1]$.

::: incremental
- Start with the **probability** $p$ - bounded at 0 and 1, e.g. 0.4
  (40%), awkward
- Turn it into **odds**,
  $\frac{p}{1-p} = \frac{probability of happening}{probability of NOT happening}$
  or $\frac{0.4}{0.6} = 0.67$ - now bounded at 0 and $+\infty$, better
- Take the **log** of that
  ($\log\left(\frac{0.4}{0.6}\right) = -0.40$) - now unbounded in both
  directions :tada:
:::

. . .

$$\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + \dots$$

- That left-hand side is the **logit**, and it ***is*** the link
  function. The right-hand side is exactly the model we have been
  fitting since week 5.
- A **logit** simply is a mathematical function that converts a
  probability (between 0 and 1) into a log-odds value that can range
  from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$
- The link-function converts the expected value of the outcome (the
  mean) into something a straight line can cope with

## Enough theory — let's fit one {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

The simplest possible version: **is a school rated below Good**, predicted
from **Progress 8** and nothing else.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
glm1 <- glm(below_good ~ P8MEA, data = model_data, family = binomial)
coef(summary(glm1))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
g0 <- as.numeric(coef(glm1)[1])
g1 <- as.numeric(coef(glm1)[2])
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
The **`Std. Error`**, **`z value`** and **`Pr(>|z|)`** columns do exactly what
their equivalents did in OLS — how precise the estimate is, and whether it is
distinguishable from zero. It is the **`Estimate`** column that needs new
thinking.
:::

## So what *is* that coefficient? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Put the estimates back into the equation from the last slide:

$$\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = `r sprintf("%.2f", g0)` + (`r sprintf("%.2f", g1)` \times \text{Progress 8})$$

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
The left-hand side is **log-odds**. So whatever is multiplying Progress 8 must
be *in log-odds too*:

> **`r sprintf("%.2f", g1)` is the amount the log-odds change for each extra
> Progress 8 point.**

One more point of Progress 8, and the log-odds of being rated below Good drop
by `r sprintf("%.2f", abs(g1))`.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
And the **intercept** is just the same thing at zero: a school with a Progress
8 of exactly 0 has log-odds of **`r sprintf("%.2f", g0)`**.
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.88em;"}
**Both of those sentences are true, and both are useless.** Nobody has an
intuition for log-odds — you cannot tell a head teacher their log-odds fell by
`r sprintf("%.2f", abs(g1))`. The next few slides are entirely about turning
this number into something you can say out loud.
:::

## Odds are not probabilities {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Worth pausing, because this trips people (including me!) up all the
time.

| Probability | Odds | In words            |
|-------------|------|---------------------|
| 0.5         | 1.0  | Evens               |
| 0.75        | 3.0  | Three to one on     |
| 0.9         | 9.0  | Nine to one on      |
| 0.1         | 0.11 | Nine to one against |

. . .

Probabilities are bounded above. **Odds are not.** That is the whole
reason we work with them.

## And odds are not odds *ratios* {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Odds** describe **one** situation

$$\text{odds} = \frac{p}{1-p}$$

*"This school's odds of being rated below Good are 0.10"*
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
**An odds ratio** compares **two**

$$\text{OR} = \frac{\text{odds}_A}{\text{odds}_B}$$

*"...which is 0.07 times the odds of a school one Progress 8 point
worse"*
:::
:::::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
- Easily the most common mistake in reading logistic output.
- The odds are the raw ingredient;
- the **ratio** is what you get when you put two of them side by side -
  and the **odds-ratio** is what a regression coefficient hands you.
:::

## Why the coefficient *is* a ratio {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

**First, where the "one" comes from.** A slope always answers the same
question, in every model you have ever fitted:

> *If the predictor goes up by **one unit**, what happens to the outcome?*

In Vol 1 that was *"one more percentage point of absence costs 0.38 Attainment
8 points"*. The **one** is not special — it is just the step size we have
always quoted coefficients in.

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
So picture **two schools, identical in every respect**, except the second has
one more unit of $x$ — one more percentage point of absence, say.
:::

## Why the coefficient *is* a ratio {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Our model says the log-odds are a straight line:

$$\log(\text{odds}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$$

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
| | Predictor | Its log-odds |
|---|---|---|
| **School A** | $x$ | $\beta_0 + \beta_1x$ |
| **School B** | $x+1$ | $\beta_0 + \beta_1x + \beta_1$ |
:::

. . .

Subtract one from the other, and everything cancels except $\beta_1$:

$$\log(\text{odds}_B) - \log(\text{odds}_A) = \beta_1$$

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
**So the coefficient is a difference of two log-odds.** Not a difference in
probability, and not a difference in odds — a difference in *logged* odds.
:::

## From a difference to a ratio {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

We have a **difference of logs**. There is a rule from school algebra for
exactly that:

$$\log(M) - \log(N) = \log\!\left(\frac{M}{N}\right)$$

[Deliberately *not* A and B — those are taken. $M$ and $N$ are just
placeholders for "whatever you are subtracting".]{style="font-size:0.8em; color:#666;"}

. . .

Ours was $\log(\text{odds}_B) - \log(\text{odds}_A)$, so $M$ is **School B's**
odds and $N$ is **School A's**:

$$\beta_1 = \log(\text{odds}_B) - \log(\text{odds}_A) = \log\!\left(\frac{\text{odds}_B}{\text{odds}_A}\right)$$

. . .

Now undo the log on both sides — exponentiate:

$$e^{\beta_1} = \frac{\text{odds}_B}{\text{odds}_A}$$

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.9em;"}
**That is the whole thing.** A ratio of two odds — because subtracting logs
*is* dividing, and the coefficient was a difference of logs all along. Nothing
was smuggled in: just a one-unit step, and one rule about logarithms.
:::

## See it in our own data {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
lo0 <- g0 + g1 * 0
od0 <- exp(lo0)
pr0 <- od0 / (1 + od0)
```

Back to the model we fitted earlier — the same two numbers:

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}

$$\log(\text{odds}) = `r sprintf("%.2f", g0)` + (`r sprintf("%.2f", g1)` \times \text{Progress 8})$$
:::

## From those two numbers to a probability {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Take a school with a Progress 8 of **0** and turn the handle. Three steps, and
each one undoes a bit of the link function:

::: {.incremental}
1.  **Log-odds** — put 0 into the equation:
    $`r sprintf("%.2f", g0)` + (`r sprintf("%.2f", g1)` \times 0) = `r sprintf("%.2f", lo0)`$
2.  **Odds** — undo the log with $\exp$:
    $e^{`r sprintf("%.2f", lo0)`} = `r sprintf("%.4f", od0)`$
3.  **Probability** — undo the odds with $\frac{\text{odds}}{1+\text{odds}}$:
    $`r sprintf("%.4f", od0)` \div `r sprintf("%.4f", 1 + od0)` = `r sprintf("%.3f", pr0)`$
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
So a school on exactly average progress has about a
**`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * pr0)` chance** of being rated below Good.
:::

## See it in our own data {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

**Every row below is those same three steps**, done at a different Progress 8
score.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Single-predictor model, so the arithmetic is visible. glm1 is already fitted
# on the "minus fifty percent" slide.
odds_at <- function(x) {
  p <- predict(glm1, newdata = data.frame(P8MEA = x), type = "response")
  as.numeric(p / (1 - p))
}
b1 <- as.numeric(coef(glm1)["P8MEA"])

tibble(
  `Progress 8`  = c(-1, 0, 1, 2),
  Probability   = sprintf("%.3f", map_dbl(c(-1, 0, 1, 2),
                    ~ as.numeric(predict(glm1, data.frame(P8MEA = .x), type = "response")))),
  Odds          = sprintf("%.4f", map_dbl(c(-1, 0, 1, 2), odds_at)),
  `Odds ÷ the row above` = c("-", sprintf("%.3f", map_dbl(c(0, 1, 2),
                    ~ odds_at(.x) / odds_at(.x - 1))))
) |> kable(align = "rrrr")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.86em"}
Check the **Progress 8 = 0** row against the slide before: probability
`r sprintf("%.3f", pr0)`, odds `r sprintf("%.4f", od0)`. The last column simply
divides each row's odds by the one above it.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
The coefficient on Progress 8 is **`r sprintf("%.2f", b1)`**, and
$e^{`r sprintf("%.2f", b1)`}$ = **`r sprintf("%.3f", exp(b1))`**.

That is the last column, every time. **One coefficient, one odds ratio,
valid wherever you start from.** Now look at the probabilities - they
fall
`r sprintf("%.2f", as.numeric(predict(glm1, data.frame(P8MEA=-1), type="response")))`
→
`r sprintf("%.2f", as.numeric(predict(glm1, data.frame(P8MEA=0), type="response")))`
→
`r sprintf("%.3f", as.numeric(predict(glm1, data.frame(P8MEA=1), type="response")))`,
doing nothing so tidy. Which is exactly why *"the probability falls by
X"* is never a safe reading of a logistic coefficient.
:::

# Binary logistic regression {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## Running the model {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Same formula interface you have used for three weeks. Two differences:
`glm()` not `lm()`, and a `family` argument.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
logit_below <- glm(
  below_good ~ P8MEA + PTFSM6CLA1A + PERCTOT + PPERSABS10 +
               log(TPUP) + PTPRIORHI + MINORGROUP,
  data   = train,
  family = binomial
)
```

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: false
ct <- summary(logit_below)$coefficients
tibble(
  Term        = rownames(ct),
  Coefficient = round(ct[, 1], 3),
  `Std. error`= round(ct[, 2], 3),
  `p`         = ifelse(ct[, 4] < 0.001, "<0.001", as.character(round(ct[, 4], 3)))
) |> kable()
```

## These coefficients are on the log-odds scale {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

- A coefficient of `r round(coef(logit_below)["P8MEA"], 2)` on Progress
  8 does **not** mean "the probability falls by
  `r abs(round(coef(logit_below)["P8MEA"], 2))`"
- It means the **log-odds** fall by that much, for every one-point
  increase in Progress 8
- Nobody thinks in log-odds. So we exponentiate, and get an **odds
  ratio**

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: true
exp(coef(logit_below)["P8MEA"])
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
**One extra Progress 8 point multiplies the odds of being rated below
Good by about `r round(exp(coef(logit_below)["P8MEA"]), 2)`** - that is,
it cuts them by roughly
`r round(100 * (1 - exp(coef(logit_below)["P8MEA"])))`%.
:::

## Reading odds ratios {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| out-width: 92%

or_tbl <- tibble(
  term = names(coef(logit_below)),
  est  = coef(logit_below),
  se   = summary(logit_below)$coefficients[, 2]
) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  mutate(or = exp(est), lo = exp(est - 1.96 * se), hi = exp(est + 1.96 * se),
         term = recode(term,
           "P8MEA" = "Progress 8",
           "PTFSM6CLA1A" = "% disadvantaged",
           "PERCTOT" = "% overall absence",
           "PPERSABS10" = "% persistently absent",
           "log(TPUP)" = "log(cohort size)",
           "PTPRIORHI" = "% high prior attainers",
           "MINORGROUPMaintained school" = "Maintained (vs academy)"))

ggplot(or_tbl, aes(x = or, y = fct_reorder(term, or))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = casa_red, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0.25, colour = casa_purple) +
  geom_point(size = 3.4, colour = casa_teal) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Odds ratio (log scale)", y = NULL,
       title = "Odds of being rated below Good",
       subtitle = "Left of the dashed line = protective; right = raises the odds")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
Anything whose interval crosses **1** is doing nothing detectable. Note
how much work Progress 8 is doing compared with everything else.
:::

## How do you score a model like this? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

For three weeks we judged models with **R²** — the share of the variation in
the outcome the model managed to explain.

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
That worked because the outcome was a *number*, with variation in it to
explain. Ours is a **yes or no**. There is no spread to account for, and R²
as you know it simply does not exist here.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
So we ask **two** questions instead, and they are genuinely different:

1.  **Does the model fit the data?** — likelihood, deviance, AIC, the
    pseudo-R²s, Hosmer–Lemeshow
2.  **Does it make good decisions?** — accuracy, the confusion matrix, ROC
    and AUC

A model can do respectably on one and badly on the other. We take them in
turn.
:::

# 1. Does the model fit? {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## Likelihood: how surprised is the model? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| label: fit-stats
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
n_tr   <- nrow(train)
ll     <- as.numeric(logLik(logit_below))
dev0   <- logit_below$null.deviance
dev1   <- logit_below$deviance
k      <- length(coef(logit_below))
cs     <- 1 - exp((dev1 - dev0) / n_tr)
cs_max <- 1 - exp(-dev0 / n_tr)
nk     <- cs / cs_max
```

Every school in the data either was or was not rated below Good. The model
assigns each one a probability. **Likelihood** asks the obvious question:

> *Given these coefficients, how probable was the data we actually saw?*

::: incremental
-   A school that *was* below Good, which the model gave 0.9 — good, that was
    likely
-   A school that was **not**, which the model gave 0.9 — bad, the model was
    confidently wrong
-   Multiply all `r comma(n_tr)` of those probabilities together and you have
    the **likelihood** of the whole dataset
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
Fitting the model *is* choosing the coefficients that make this number as
large as possible — **maximum likelihood**. We report its log, because
multiplying `r comma(n_tr)` probabilities together gives a number too small
for a computer to hold.

For our model: **log-likelihood = `r sprintf("%.1f", ll)`**. Always negative;
closer to zero is better.
:::

## Deviance: distance from a perfect fit {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

A log-likelihood on its own is hard to read. **Deviance** rescales it into
something more like an error score — *how far this model sits from one that
predicted every school perfectly*.

$$\text{deviance} = -2 \times \text{log-likelihood}$$

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
| | | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| **Null deviance** | `r sprintf("%.1f", dev0)` | with **no predictors at all** — just the overall rate |
| **Residual deviance** | `r sprintf("%.1f", dev1)` | with our seven predictors in |
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**Lower is better**, and the drop — `r sprintf("%.0f", dev0 - dev1)` — is what
the predictors bought us. This is the direct equivalent of the sum-of-squares
drop you used to read off an OLS table.
:::

::: {.notes}
Deviance is also the statistic behind the overdispersion check later in the
Poisson section: residual deviance divided by residual degrees of freedom.
Worth flagging forward so it is not a surprise there.
:::

## AIC: fit, minus a fine for complexity {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

There is a problem with judging a model on deviance alone: **adding any
predictor, however useless, will always lower it slightly.** Left to itself,
deviance always says "more variables".

. . .

So we charge for them:

$$\text{AIC} = \text{deviance} + 2k \quad\text{where } k = \text{number of coefficients}$$

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
For our model: `r sprintf("%.1f", dev1)` + 2 × `r k` =
**`r sprintf("%.1f", dev1 + 2*k)`**. A predictor only improves the AIC if it
reduces the deviance by more than the 2 points it costs.
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.86em;"}
**AIC has no meaning on its own.** `r sprintf("%.0f", AIC(logit_below))` is
neither good nor bad — it is only useful for **comparing models fitted to the
same data**. Lower wins. That is exactly how we used it earlier to choose
between a raw and a logged predictor.
:::

## The pseudo-R²s {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

People badly want an R², so several substitutes exist. The two you will meet
in software output:

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**Cox & Snell** — built from the likelihood ratio between your model and the
null model. For us: **`r sprintf("%.3f", cs)`**.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
That looks dismal — until you learn its catch. **Cox & Snell cannot reach 1.**
With a binary outcome its ceiling here is **`r sprintf("%.3f", cs_max)`**, so
`r sprintf("%.3f", cs)` is really `r sprintf("%.3f", cs)` out of a possible
`r sprintf("%.3f", cs_max)`.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**Nagelkerke** fixes precisely that, by dividing by the ceiling:

$$R^2_{\text{Nagelkerke}} = \frac{`r sprintf("%.3f", cs)`}{`r sprintf("%.3f", cs_max)`} = \mathbf{`r sprintf("%.3f", nk)`}$$

Now it can reach 1, and it reads much more like the R² you are used to.
:::

## ...and how much to trust them {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
Report them if the journal or the marker expects them — but know what you are
saying.

::: incremental
-   **They are not "variance explained".** Nothing here is variance. The name
    is borrowed, and the interpretation does not come with it
-   **They are not comparable across datasets**, and barely across models. A
    Nagelkerke of 0.32 is not "half as good" as one of 0.64
-   **There is no accepted threshold** for a good one. Values that would be
    embarrassing in OLS are routine here
:::
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.86em;"}
Treat a pseudo-R² as a **rough indication that the predictors are doing
something**, and nothing more. If you want to know whether the model is
actually any use, ask the second question — the one we come to next.
:::

# 2. Does it make good decisions? {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## Don't mark your own homework {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

The obvious way to answer that is to run the model over our schools and count
how often it got the answer right.

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**The problem: it has already seen those schools.** The coefficients were
chosen to fit them as closely as possible. Scoring a model on the data it was
fitted to is revising with the exam paper in front of you — you will do well,
and it tells you nothing about the next paper.
:::

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
# Split the schools in two, before fitting anything
set.seed(42)
train_idx <- sample(nrow(model_data), floor(0.7 * nrow(model_data)))
train <- model_data[train_idx, ]   # fit the model on these
test  <- model_data[-train_idx, ]  # judge it on these
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
`r comma(nrow(train))` schools to **learn** from, `r comma(nrow(test))` kept
back to **test** on. The model never sees the second group while it is being
fitted, so how it does there is a fair sitting of a fresh paper.

That is what **test-set accuracy** means: of the `r comma(nrow(test))` schools
it had never met, what share did it classify correctly?
:::

## So how good is it? {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
p_below <- predict(logit_below, newdata = test, type = "response")
accuracy <- mean((p_below > 0.5) == test$below_good)
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
baseline <- max(mean(test$below_good), 1 - mean(test$below_good))
auc_below <- auc_of(p_below, test$below_good)
```

::: {style="font-size: 1.1em"}
**Test-set accuracy: `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * accuracy)`**
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 1.1em"}
Not bad! Nearly nine schools in ten classified correctly.
:::

. . .

::: {.fragment style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #C94C4C"}
**Now watch.**
:::

## The single most important slide today {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| out-width: 90%

tibble(
  model = c("Our logistic model", "A model that always\nsays 'not below Good'"),
  acc   = c(accuracy, baseline)
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_rev(model), y = 100 * acc, fill = model)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * acc)), hjust = -0.15, size = 6) +
  coord_flip(ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(casa_teal, casa_red)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Test-set accuracy (%)",
       title = "Our model versus a model that does nothing at all") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
A model that makes **the same prediction every single time**, with no
data at all, scores `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * baseline)`. Our model
beats it by **`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * (accuracy - baseline))`
percentage points**.
:::

## Why accuracy lied to us {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
cm <- table(Actual = ifelse(test$below_good == 1, "Below Good", "Good or better"),
            Predicted = ifelse(p_below > 0.5, "Below Good", "Good or better"))

# kable() silently drops the dimnames of a table object, which leaves the
# reader with two identical sets of labels and no way to tell which axis is
# which. Rebuilt as a data frame so the headings say so explicitly.
tibble::tibble(
  ` ` = paste("**Actually**", rownames(cm)),
  `Predicted below Good`     = as.integer(cm[, "Below Good"]),
  `Predicted Good or better` = as.integer(cm[, "Good or better"])
) |>
  kable(align = "lrr")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em"}
The `r comma(nrow(test))` **test** schools — the ones the model never saw
while it was being fitted.
:::

::: incremental
- Only **`r comma(sum(test$below_good))`** of the `r comma(nrow(test))`
  test schools are actually below Good - the class is **rare**
- The model catches **`r cm["Below Good", "Below Good"]`** of them and
  misses **`r cm["Below Good", "Good or better"]`**
- If you were Ofsted, trying to decide which schools to visit, this
  model would be close to useless *at this threshold*
:::

. . .

**Always, always compare your accuracy against the majority-class
baseline.** On imbalanced data, accuracy on its own is not evidence of
anything.

## 0.5 was a choice, not a law {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

The model does not output yes or no. It outputs a **probability** for every
school. We turned that into a yes/no by flagging anything above **0.5** — and
nothing made 0.5 the right number.

```{r}
#| label: threshold-table
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
thr_tbl <- map_dfr(c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1), function(t) {
  flag <- p_below > t
  tibble(`Flag if probability above` = sprintf("%.2f", t),
         `Struggling schools caught`  = sum(flag & test$below_good == 1),
         `...and missed`              = sum(!flag & test$below_good == 1),
         `False alarms`               = sum(flag & test$below_good == 0))
})
kable(thr_tbl, align = "crrr")
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
Drop the threshold and you catch far more struggling schools — **32 up to
121** of the `r comma(sum(test$below_good))`. But the false alarms go from
**23 to 316**.

**There is no setting that is simply best.** Which error hurts more is a
policy question, and the model cannot answer it for you.
:::

## Every threshold at once: the ROC curve {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Rather than argue about one cut-off, plot **all of them**. Two numbers per
threshold:

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
- **True positive rate** — of the schools that *really are* below Good, what
  share did we flag? *(we want this high)*
- **False positive rate** — of the schools that are *fine*, what share did we
  flag anyway? *(we want this low)*
:::

```{r}
#| label: roc-explained
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 6.2
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-align: center
thr_all <- seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 400)
roc_df <- map_dfr(thr_all, function(t) {
  tibble(tpr = mean(p_below[test$below_good == 1] > t),
         fpr = mean(p_below[test$below_good == 0] > t))
})
marks <- map_dfr(c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1), function(t) {
  tibble(t = t,
         tpr = mean(p_below[test$below_good == 1] > t),
         fpr = mean(p_below[test$below_good == 0] > t))
})

ggplot(roc_df, aes(fpr, tpr)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(colour = casa_teal, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = marks, colour = casa_red, size = 2.6) +
  geom_text(data = marks, aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", t)),
            hjust = -0.35, size = 3.2, colour = casa_red) +
  labs(x = "False positive rate", y = "True positive rate") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
**Each red dot is one row of the table above.** Sweep the threshold from 1
down to 0 and you trace the whole curve. The dashed diagonal is what you would
get by **guessing at random** — the further above it you sit, the more the
model knows.
:::

## And AUC is the area underneath it {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
One curve is awkward to quote in a sentence, so we summarise it by the **area
under it** — the *AUC*.
:::

| AUC | What it means |
|---|---|
| **0.5** | the diagonal — no better than tossing a coin |
| **0.7–0.8** | useful |
| **0.9+** | very strong |
| **1.0** | perfect: every struggling school scored above every healthy one |

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
It also has a reading that needs no curve at all:

> **Pick one struggling school and one healthy school at random. AUC is the
> probability the model gives the struggling one the higher score.**
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.88em;"}
Notice what that does **not** depend on: any threshold. AUC asks whether the
model puts schools in the right **order**, which is a different and fairer
question from whether it labels them correctly at one arbitrary cut-off.
:::

## But the model is not useless {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Accuracy asks "did you get it right?" at one arbitrary cut-off. A better
question is "**do you rank schools sensibly?**"

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.3
#| out-width: 95%

thr <- seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 300)
roc <- map_dfr(thr, function(t) {
  tibble(tpr = mean(p_below[test$below_good == 1] > t),
         fpr = mean(p_below[test$below_good == 0] > t))
})

p_roc <- ggplot(roc, aes(fpr, tpr)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(colour = casa_teal, linewidth = 1.3) +
  labs(x = "False positive rate", y = "True positive rate",
       title = sprintf("ROC curve - AUC = %.3f", auc_below))

p_box <- tibble(p = p_below,
                actual = ifelse(test$below_good == 1, "Below Good", "Good or better")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = actual, y = p, fill = actual)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.75, outlier.alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = casa_red) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(casa_pink, casa_teal)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Predicted probability",
       title = "Predictions, by what actually happened") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p_roc + p_box
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
**AUC = `r sprintf("%.3f", auc_below)`** - pick a below-Good school and
a Good-or-better school at random, and the model gives the below-Good
one a higher score `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * auc_below)` of the time.
That is genuinely useful. The problem was never the model - it was the
**0.5 threshold**, which is a choice, not a law.
:::

## Moving the threshold {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.3
#| out-width: 95%

sweep <- map_dfr(seq(0.02, 0.9, by = 0.01), function(t) {
  pred <- p_below > t
  tibble(threshold = t,
         `Caught (recall)`   = mean(pred[test$below_good == 1]),
         `Correct when flagged (precision)` =
            ifelse(sum(pred) == 0, NA, mean(test$below_good[pred] == 1)))
}) |>
  pivot_longer(-threshold)

ggplot(sweep, aes(threshold, value, colour = name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(casa_purple, casa_teal), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Classification threshold", y = NULL,
       title = "There is no free lunch here") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
Drop the threshold and you catch more struggling schools, but more of
your flags are false alarms. **Which error is worse is a policy
question, not a statistical one** - and that is the right way round.
:::

## A second outcome, same story {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
logit_out <- glm(
  outstanding ~ P8MEA + PTFSM6CLA1A + PERCTOT + PPERSABS10 +
                log(TPUP) + PTPRIORHI + MINORGROUP,
  data = train, family = binomial)
p_out <- predict(logit_out, newdata = test, type = "response")
acc_out <- mean((p_out > 0.5) == test$outstanding)
base_out <- max(mean(test$outstanding), 1 - mean(test$outstanding))
auc_out <- auc_of(p_out, test$outstanding)

tibble(
  Model = c("Below Good vs Good+", "Outstanding vs rest"),
  Accuracy = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * c(accuracy, acc_out)),
  Baseline = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * c(baseline, base_out)),
  AUC = sprintf("%.3f", c(auc_below, auc_out)),
  `Caught at p > 0.5` = c(
    sprintf("%d of %d", cm["Below Good", "Below Good"], sum(test$below_good)),
    sprintf("%d of %d", sum(p_out > 0.5 & test$outstanding == 1), sum(test$outstanding)))
) |> kable()
```

. . .

- Higher AUC, so the ranking is even better
- Barely above baseline on accuracy, and still catching well under half
  the Outstanding schools
- **Not a quirk of one model.** This is what rare outcomes do, and you
  will meet it in your own data

## An uncomfortable question {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Progress 8 is by far the strongest predictor in both models. So what
have we actually built?

::: incremental
- Ofsted inspectors **read a school's Progress 8 score before they
  visit**
- So we are not independently predicting a judgement - we are partly
  **recovering one of Ofsted's own inputs**
- That is circularity, and it makes the model much less interesting than
  it first looked
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
And a second problem: inspection dates in this file run from
**`r min(model_data$insp_year, na.rm = TRUE)` to
`r max(model_data$insp_year, na.rm = TRUE)`**, median
`r median(model_data$insp_year, na.rm = TRUE)`. Some of these ratings
were handed out a decade before the results we are using to "predict"
them.

**Ask these questions of your own models.** They matter more than
another decimal place of AUC.
:::

# Wrapping up {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## The three you did not get today {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Everything we have done generalises, and **the hard part is behind you**. Each
of these is the same machinery with a different family:

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
| If your outcome is... | Use | And the coefficients are |
|---|---|---|
| An **ordered** category — Ofsted's four grades, a Likert scale | `MASS::polr()` | odds of landing in a *higher* category |
| An **unordered** category — which region, which destination | `nnet::multinom()` | odds against a reference category |
| A **count** — pupils excluded, schools below Good in an LA | `glm(family = poisson)` | **rate ratios**, read just like odds ratios |
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
Two things to know if you reach for the count model:

-   An **offset** — `offset(log(pupils))` — turns a model of counts into a
    model of *rates*, which is almost always what you want
-   Check for **overdispersion** (residual deviance ÷ residual df). Much above
    1 and you want `quasipoisson` or `MASS::glm.nb()`
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.85em;"}
**The practical covers these**, and the reading goes further. You already have
the two ideas that make them work: a **link function**, and coefficients you
have to **exponentiate** before they mean anything.
:::

## The family, in one slide {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

| Outcome | `family =` | Link | Interpret coefficients as |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Continuous | `gaussian` | identity | Units of y per unit of x |
| Yes / no | `binomial` | logit | Odds ratios |
| x out of n | `binomial` | logit | Odds ratios |
| Ordered categories | `MASS::polr()` | logit | Odds of being in a higher category |
| Unordered categories | `nnet::multinom()` | logit | Odds vs a reference category |
| Count | `poisson` | log | Rate ratios |
| Overdispersed count | `MASS::glm.nb()` | log | Rate ratios |

. . .

**One framework.** Change the family, change the link, and everything
you learned about building and interpreting a linear model still
applies.

## What carried over, and what didn't {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Still true**

- The recipe: start simple, add complexity that earns its place
- Confounding, mediation, interactions
- Multicollinearity and VIF
- Thinking hard about what belongs in the model
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Different now**

- No R² - use AIC, deviance, or predictive performance
- Coefficients need exponentiating before they mean anything
- Residual plots look strange and need different diagnostics
- Accuracy is a trap on imbalanced outcomes
:::
:::::

## Where you can go next {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

- **Generalised additive models (GAMs)** - when the relationship is
  smooth but not a straight line
- **`glmer()`** - the intersection of this week and last week: a GLM
  with random effects, for grouped non-normal data
- **Spatial and geographically weighted regression** - when the
  relationship itself varies over space
- **Ridge and lasso** - when you have too many predictors and need the
  model to choose

. . .

You now have the two big extensions to OLS: last week we relaxed
**independence**, this week we relaxed **normality**. Almost everything
else is a combination of the two.

## Conclusions {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

- **Look at your outcome variable before you choose a model.** Week 1's
  data types were not an academic exercise - they determine what you are
  allowed to do
- A GLM is not a new method, it is the same linear predictor with a
  different distribution and a link function bolted on
- **Always compare against a baseline.** A model that beats "predict the
  majority every time" by half a percentage point has not learned much
- Check your assumptions, and remember the threshold is a choice you
  make rather than one the model makes for you
- And ask where your predictors came from. Our best one turned out to be
  something Ofsted had already read

## Today's Practical {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

- Building and interpreting your own logistic and Poisson models on the
  schools data
- Practice at the bit that matters most: **interpreting odds ratios and
  rate ratios** in plain English
- And deciding, for an outcome of your own choosing, which member of the
  family you actually need
